skills.name: State what they like about themselves as God's creation and list chores they do at home
skills.mastery: States good things about himself or herself (my eyes, my voice, I can run, I help others) as made by God (Psalm 139:13: you knit me together in my mother's womb), and lists five chores done at home (sweeping, washing utensils, fetching water, making the bed, feeding animals). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Knowing one is unique as God made one, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.
Stating one's gender as God created. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks there is nothing good about himself because he is not the best in class.

example.question: Name one thing you like about yourself.
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, I am not the best
example.correct_answer: My smile (I can sing, I help my friends)

misconceptions.cause: The child compares himself with the top pupils.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, I am not the best" beside "My smile (I can sing, I help my friends)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Read Psalm 139:13-14. Let each child say one good thing about a classmate, then about himself.
misconceptions.feedback: God made you and there is good in you. Name one thing you like.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher of the school's own tradition (FAITH: the wording touches belief or practice): a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only looks (fair skin, nice clothes) are good things about a person.

example.question: Is being kind something to like about yourself?
example.wrong_answer: No, only how I look counts
example.correct_answer: Yes, kindness is a good thing about me

misconceptions.cause: Praise at home is often about looks.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only how I look counts" beside "Yes, kindness is a good thing about me" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: List good things we cannot see: kind, brave, helpful.
misconceptions.feedback: Being kind and helpful are good things about you too.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lists playing or watching TV as chores.

example.question: Which is a chore: sweeping or watching TV?

misconceptions.cause: Chore is a new word.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Watching TV" beside "Sweeping" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: A chore is a job that helps at home. Sort cards into chores and play.
misconceptions.feedback: Sweeping is a chore. Watching TV is not.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks liking yourself means saying you are better than others.

example.question: Does liking yourself mean you are better than others?
example.correct_answer: No, everyone is special to God

misconceptions.cause: Self-praise is heard as boasting.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes" beside "No, everyone is special to God" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say: God made each person special; liking yourself and others go together.
misconceptions.feedback: You are special and so is everyone else.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Name members of the family, nuclear and extended (Acts 10:2)
skills.mastery: Names family members (father, mother, brothers, sisters) and the extended family (grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins), says belonging to a family gives love and help, and that Cornelius and all his family worshipped God together (Acts 10:2). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

Praying with family members. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.

skills.name: State items shared at home and four items that should not be shared for healthy living
skills.mastery: States items a family shares (food, utensils in turn after washing, chairs, the table, water, books, a radio or TV) to foster unity, and four items that should not be shared for health (toothbrush, towel, comb, underwear, handkerchief, razor blade), because they carry germs from one person to another. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Items shared at home, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.
Items shared at home as a family. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.

misconceptions.error: Counts neighbours or friends as members of the extended family.

example.question: Is your neighbour part of your extended family?
example.correct_answer: No, the extended family is relatives like grandparents and cousins

misconceptions.cause: Close neighbours are called aunt or uncle.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes" beside "No, the extended family is relatives like grandparents and cousins" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Draw the family tree. Neighbours are not on it, though we love them.
misconceptions.feedback: The extended family is relatives: grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks grandparents are not family because they live far away.

example.question: Your grandmother lives in the village. Is she your family?
example.correct_answer: Yes, she is in my extended family

misconceptions.cause: Family is pictured as people at home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, she lives far" beside "Yes, she is in my extended family" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Put grandparents on the tree above parents.
misconceptions.feedback: Grandparents are family wherever they live.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks Cornelius worshipped God alone.

example.question: According to Acts 10:2, who worshipped God with Cornelius?

misconceptions.cause: Bible people are often pictured alone.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nobody" beside "All his family" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Read Acts 10:2 together.
misconceptions.feedback: Cornelius and all his family worshipped God together.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a cousin a sister.

example.question: Your uncle's daughter is your...?

misconceptions.cause: Cousins are called sisters at home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sister" beside "Cousin" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Trace the line on the tree from uncle to his daughter.
misconceptions.feedback: Your uncle's daughter is your cousin.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sharing a toothbrush with a sibling is kind.

example.question: Should brothers share one toothbrush?
example.correct_answer: No, a toothbrush should not be shared

misconceptions.cause: Sharing is always praised.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, sharing is good" beside "No, a toothbrush should not be shared" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say: some things carry germs from mouth to mouth. Kindness is giving your sibling his own.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not share a toothbrush. It spreads germs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a razor blade can be shared if it looks clean.

example.question: Can a family share one razor blade?
example.correct_answer: No, it can spread blood-borne disease

misconceptions.cause: The danger cannot be seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, if it looks clean" beside "No, it can spread blood-borne disease" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show the "never share" list. Blood can carry diseases.
misconceptions.feedback: Never share a razor blade. It can spread disease.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher and the school counsellor (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks nothing at home should be shared, so food is kept for oneself.

example.question: Should a family share food?

misconceptions.cause: The no-share rule is over-learnt.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, each keeps his own" beside "Yes, sharing food brings unity" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Sort into share (food, chairs) and do not share (toothbrush, towel).
misconceptions.feedback: Families share food, chairs and water. Only personal items are not shared.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a towel can be shared because it is washed.

example.question: Is a bathing towel shared or not?

misconceptions.cause: Washing seems to make anything shareable.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Shared, it is washed" beside "Not shared" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: A towel touches the body and can pass skin infections.
misconceptions.feedback: A bathing towel is personal. Do not share it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creation of the sky, sun, moon, and stars
content_topics: Specific learning outcomes By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
list the importance of reading the Bible
state how often they read the Bible
appreciate the Bible as a guide in daily life

observe the sky and tell what they see during the day and at night,
draw and colour the sun, moon, and stars,
cut and mount pictures of the sun, moon, and stars on a chart,
sing a song on creation, ‘Bwana Mungu nashangaa kabisa...........,
in groups, write the verse in Genesis 1:16 on flashcards and display it in class.

Responsibility is portrayed as learners write Genesis 1:16 on flashcards and display it in class. Respect is demonstrated as learners perform tasks in groups and respect each other’s opinions. Link to other activity areas:

Creative Activities: learners sing the song, ‘My Bible and I’.

skills.name: Recognise God as the creator of the sky, sun, moon and stars (Genesis 1:14-19)
skills.mastery: Says God made the lights in the sky on the fourth day (Genesis 1:14-19): the sun to rule the day, the moon to rule the night, and the stars; they mark days, seasons and years; God saw that it was good. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CRE.G2.RUBRIC.1.1, CRE.G2.RUBRIC.1.2, CRE.G2.RUBRIC.1.3, CRE.G2.RUBRIC.1.4, CRE.G2.RUBRIC.1.5, CRE.G2.RUBRIC.1.6), never as a phone question: b) draw the sun, moon, and stars to appreciate God’s creation.

skills.mastery: Lists why Christians read the Bible: it is God's word, it guides how to live (Psalm 119:105: your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path), it teaches about God and Jesus, it comforts and helps us pray; and says families can read it together. misconceptions.error: Thinks people or scientists made the sun and stars.

example.question: Who created the sun, moon and stars?

misconceptions.cause: Lights the child knows (bulbs) are made by people.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "People" beside "God" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Read Genesis 1:16. People make bulbs; God made the sun.
misconceptions.feedback: God created the sun, moon and stars.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher of the school's own tradition (FAITH: the wording touches belief or practice): a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says the sun was made on the first day.

example.question: On which day did God make the sun, moon and stars?

misconceptions.cause: Light was made on day one, so the sun seems to come first.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The first day" beside "The fourth day" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Count the days of creation on fingers to four.
misconceptions.feedback: God made the sun, moon and stars on the fourth day.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the sun rules the night and the moon the day.

example.question: Which light rules the night?

misconceptions.cause: The two are mixed up.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The sun" beside "The moon" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Draw a day sky and a night sky and place each light.
misconceptions.feedback: The sun rules the day and the moon rules the night.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the stars are only decorations with no purpose.

example.question: What are the lights in the sky for, says Genesis 1:14?
example.correct_answer: To mark days, seasons and years and give light

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only to look nice" beside "To mark days, seasons and years and give light" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Read Genesis 1:14 and link with days and seasons.
misconceptions.feedback: The lights in the sky mark days, seasons and years.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only pastors and adults need to read the Bible.

example.question: Can children read the Bible too?
example.correct_answer: Yes, children and families can read it

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the Bible read by leaders.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only pastors" beside "Yes, children and families can read it" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a children's Bible and read a verse together.
misconceptions.feedback: Children can read the Bible too.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks Psalm 119:105 means the Bible gives real light like a lamp.

example.question: What does "your word is a lamp for my feet" mean?
example.correct_answer: God's word shows us the right way to live

misconceptions.cause: Young children take words literally.

misconceptions.help: Walk a dark path with a torch: it shows where to step. God's word shows how to live.
misconceptions.feedback: God's word shows us the right way, like a lamp shows the path.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks we read the Bible only for nice stories.

example.question: Why do Christians read the Bible?
example.correct_answer: To learn about God and how to live

misconceptions.cause: Bible lessons are often stories.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "For fun stories only" beside "To learn about God and how to live" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Name a story and its lesson for life.
misconceptions.feedback: We read the Bible to learn about God and how to live.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher of the school's own tradition (FAITH: the wording touches belief or practice): a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the Bible should be read only on Sunday.

example.question: When can a family read the Bible?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only on Sunday" beside "Any day" and ask the child to choose.

misconceptions.feedback: A family can read the Bible every day.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

mention the lesson learnt from the call of Samuel
desire to obey God’s commandments

skills.name: Retell the call of Samuel and mention the lesson from it (1 Samuel 3:3-10)
skills.mastery: Retells 1 Samuel 3:3-10: the boy Samuel was sleeping in the house of the Lord; the Lord called "Samuel!"; three times he ran to Eli thinking Eli called; Eli understood it was the Lord and told him to answer; the Lord called again and Samuel said "Speak, for your servant is listening." Lesson: listen to God and obey, and answer when called. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Ways of having a good relationship with God, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.
The importance of obeying parents. Proposed, to confirm by a CRE teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks it was Eli who called Samuel each time.

example.question: Who was calling Samuel?

misconceptions.cause: Samuel himself thought so.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Eli" beside "The Lord (God)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Read 1 Samuel 3:8. Eli understood it was the Lord.
misconceptions.feedback: It was the Lord calling Samuel, not Eli.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks God called only once.

example.question: How many times did Samuel run to Eli?

misconceptions.cause: The repetition is not remembered.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Once" beside "Three times" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Act it out with three runs.
misconceptions.feedback: Samuel ran to Eli three times before he knew it was God.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CRE teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives Samuel's answer as "I am sleeping" or "Who is it?".

example.question: What did Samuel say when God called the last time?
